title: Judith Calls the Elders to Account
sum: Only now, after seven chapters of empire and siege, does the heroine appear. Judith is a widow of Bethulia, of the tribe of Simeon, rich, beautiful and devout. For more than three years she has lived in a tent on her roof, fasting every day except the Sabbaths, new moons and feasts. No one speaks ill of her.

When she hears that Uzziah has promised to surrender in five days if God does not help, she summons the elders. Her speech is the theological heart of the book. To set God a deadline is to put him to the test. No one can search out God's mind; he may save or destroy as he wills, and the right response is to wait, pray and give thanks, for he is testing them as he tested Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Uzziah admits she is right but cannot break his oath, and asks her to pray for rain. She answers that she will do something that will be told for generations, and asks them not to ask what.
readings: Read as theology

Judith's speech (8:11–27) sets out a theology of trust under siege: God is free, people may not bargain with him, and suffering may be a test rather than a punishment. The rest of the book shows that theology at work.
Read as a portrait

The narrator builds Judith slowly: genealogy, widowhood, fasting, wealth, beauty, reputation. Each detail will matter. Her beauty becomes her weapon, her piety its limit, her wealth her freedom to act alone.

views.C: Catholic readers have long held Judith up as a model of prayer, penance and trust in Providence. Her refusal to put God to the test agrees with Catholic teaching that tempting God is a sin against the virtue of religion (Aquinas, Summa II-II q.97). Her life of fasting and her rooftop retreat were read as a pattern for widows and religious.
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in Judith's widowhood, fasting and prayer the ascetic life the church still keeps in its fasts. Her refusal to keep fasts on Sabbaths and feast days matches the Orthodox rule against strict fasting on Saturdays and Sundays.
views.P: Protestant readers who do not take Judith as Scripture can still admire this speech. Its teaching, that God may not be put to the test and that hardship is a Father's discipline, agrees with Deuteronomy 6:16 and Hebrews 12:5–11, so they could read it "for example of life".
views.H: Scholars note the careful build-up of the heroine and the sharp irony: the elders, who should lead, despair; a woman, who has no office, gives the sermon. The genealogy links her to Simeon, preparing for 9:2. The speech's teaching that idol worship is a thing of the past (8:18–20) fits a writer after the exile, and the book's readers after the Maccabean crisis.
views.J: In Jewish thought, Judith's refusal to "test" God echoes Deuteronomy 6:16, and her teaching that God tests the righteous is close to the rabbinic comment on Psalm 11:5 that God tests the righteous and not the wicked, as a potter tests only sound jars (Genesis Rabbah 55:2). The medieval Hebrew retellings kept her as a pious widow.

deep.b:
Judith uses one Greek verb in two directions. The elders "put God to the test" (8:12) by giving him five days; but God "is testing us, just as he tested our ancestors" (8:25). The difference is who sets the terms. When Israel at Massah demanded water, Exodus says "they put the LORD on trial, saying, 'Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?'" (Exodus 17:7), and Deuteronomy forbids it: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16). Bethulia's thirst is a second Massah, and Uzziah's oath repeats the old demand.

Judith's answer has three steps. First, God's mind cannot be searched (8:13–14), so no one may name the day when he must act. Second, God is free to save or to destroy (8:15–16); he is not a man to be threatened or bargained with. Third, the people have not worshiped idols (8:18–20), so the siege is not punishment; it is testing, and it calls for thanks (8:25–27). Thomas Aquinas, in his question on tempting God, explains that a person tempts God when he demands a sign of God's power or knowledge without need (Summa II-II q.97 a.1–2), and the elders' five days are such a demand. Whether God sends suffering or only permits it, and whether suffering is discipline, are carded at Job 2, Job 5 and Job 36.

Judith fasts "every day of her widowhood" except on the Sabbaths, new moons and feasts and the day before each (8:6). This is a rule of life, not a fast for one crisis. Israel's law commanded only one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31); the prophets and the books after the exile add fasts for mourning and repentance (Zechariah 8:19; Ezra 8:21; Esther 4:16). By the first century some Jews fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays instead (Didache 8:1). Judith's exceptions show that fasting must give way to joy on holy days. The churches still differ over whether Christians should keep fixed fast days; their views are set out in the card below. On fasting in 4:9–15, see the notes on chapter 4.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:16; Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 23:19; Genesis 22:1; Deuteronomy 8:2–5; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11; Job 11:7; 1 Corinthians 2:11; Romans 11:33–34; Luke 2:36–38; 1 Timothy 5:5; Matthew 4:7; Numbers 1:6

settings.to: Uzziah, Chabris and Charmis, the elders of Bethulia, whom she has summoned to her house
settings.when: after Uzziah swore to surrender the town if no help came in five days (7:30–31)
settings.why: To show the elders that their oath tested God, and to call them from despair to trust, thanks and an example for the people. Inside the story she speaks as a private woman correcting the town's rulers; that reversal is part of the point.
settings.readers: Most scholars: Jews in Judea under the Hasmonean high priests and kings, about 150–100 BC. They remembered how Antiochus IV had defiled the Temple (167 BC) and how the Maccabees had won it back, and their own rulers were pushing north into Samaria and Galilee, where Bethulia is set. They had lived through a time when some Jews thought God had abandoned them, and others kept faith under persecution and waited for God to act (1 Maccabees 1–2; Daniel 11:32–35). Judith's speech taught them that God's delays are tests, not abandonment, and that no one may set him terms.
views: Most readers, Jewish and Christian, take the speech as sound teaching on trust in God.

The Hasmonean date is the majority view, not a settled one, and no copy of Judith was found at Qumran. Some scholars place the book at the end of the Persian period, others early in the Maccabean revolt (see the book introduction).
Many scholars stress that the book gives its theology to a woman, while the male leaders fail.

settings.to: Judith, with the other elders present
settings.when: after her rebuke
settings.why: To admit she is right and to excuse the oath as forced on him by the people, and to ask her, as a devout woman, to pray for rain.

settings.when: after Uzziah asks her to pray for rain
settings.why: To promise an act of deliverance within the five days, to arrange to leave the town that night, and to forbid questions until it is done.

settings.when: as they leave her tent
settings.why: To send her off with a blessing: "Go in peace, and may the Lord God go before you."

traditions.q: Judith fasted every day except Sabbaths, new moons and feasts (8:6). Should Christians keep fixed fast days?
views: Yes. The church keeps Wednesdays and Fridays as fast days through most of the year, and four fasting seasons, above all Great Lent. The Didache already told Christians to fast on Wednesday and Friday (Didache 8:1). The Apostolic Canons require clergy and laity to keep the fast of Lent and of Wednesday and Friday (Canon 69), and forbid fasting on Sunday or Saturday, except Holy Saturday (Canon 64). Like Judith's, the rule gives way on the feasts.

Yes, with set days. Every Friday and the season of Lent are penitential days. Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence, and Fridays are days of abstinence from meat unless a solemnity falls on them; bishops' conferences may let other works of penance take the place of abstinence (Code of Canon Law 1249–1253). Paul VI's Paenitemini (1966) set out these rules and taught that penance must be inward as well as outward.

Fasting is good, fixed laws about it are not. The Augsburg Confession (article 26) praises fasting as a bodily discipline that helps a Christian serve, but rejects traditions about foods and days that are imposed on consciences as necessary or as earning grace.

Fasting is for special occasions, not a calendar. Calvin commends public and private fasts in times of calamity, for prayer and humility, but rejects Lent as a superstitious imitation of Christ (Institutes 4.12.14–21). The Westminster Confession lists "solemn fastings" among the parts of worship "upon special occasions" (21.5).

Yes, in the Prayer Book. The Book of Common Prayer (1662) keeps "A Table of the Vigils, Fasts, and Days of Fasting or Abstinence": the forty days of Lent, the Ember Days, the Rogation Days and all the Fridays in the year, except Christmas Day.

title: Judith's Prayer
sum: Before acting, Judith prays. She puts ashes on her head and sackcloth on her body, and at the hour when the evening incense is offered in Jerusalem she cries out to God. She remembers her ancestor Simeon, whose sword avenged the rape of Dinah, and asks the God who planned all history to break the pride of the Assyrians, who trust in horses and weapons and plan to defile his sanctuary.

She asks for something few prayers ask: that God will strike down the enemy "by the deceit of my lips", and break their pride "by a woman's hand". God is the God of the lowly, the helper of the weak, the rescuer of the hopeless. Let all nations know that there is no other protector of Israel.
readings: Read as a psalm

The prayer is built like a psalm of lament: an appeal to God's past acts (9:2–4), his foreknowledge (9:5–6), the enemy's pride (9:7–8), a plea (9:9–10, 13), and praise of the God of the weak (9:11–14).
Read as a war prayer

Judith asks for vengeance and victory, as Moses and Deborah sang. Her models are Simeon and Levi at Shechem. The prayer asks God to bless both violence and deceit, and that has made it one of the hardest passages in the book.

views.C: Catholic tradition has prized the prayer as a model of humble trust: God saves by the weak (9:11). Thomas Aquinas, holding that every lie is a sin, teaches that Judith is praised not for her deceit but for her desire to save her people, and for risking her life (Summa II-II q.110 a.3 ad 3). Jerome's Latin softens the plea for "deceit".
views.O: Orthodox readers read the prayer with the Psalms, as the cry of the humble to the God who "shatters wars", and its timing with the Temple incense as a model of joining personal prayer to the church's worship.
views.P: Protestant readers have praised the prayer's trust in God; some have counted its plea for deceit and its praise of Simeon (against Genesis 49:5–7) among the book's moral difficulties.
views.H: Scholars read the prayer as a key to the book's ideals: zeal for purity like the Maccabees' (1 Maccabees 2:24–26), the theme of the weak hand, and the Greek of Exodus 15:3. The praise of Simeon at Shechem matches Jubilees 30 and suits the Hasmonean wars against the Samaritans of Shechem.
views.J: Jewish retellings of Shechem in Jubilees 30 and the Testament of Levi likewise praise Simeon and Levi for zeal against defilement, against Jacob's curse. The medieval Hebrew Judith stories kept the prayer's spirit, setting her deed in the time of the Maccabees.

deep.b:
Judith begins with Genesis 34. Shechem son of Hamor rapes Dinah, then seeks to marry her. Her brothers answer "with trickery", demanding that the men of Shechem be circumcised, and on the third day, while the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill them all (Genesis 34:13, 25). Jacob rebukes them, and on his deathbed he curses their anger: "Their anger be cursed, for it was savage, / their rage, for it was relentless" (Genesis 49:7). Judith instead says that God gave Simeon the sword (9:2). Here her prayer conflicts with Genesis' own verdict.

Judith was not the only one to praise the brothers. Jubilees 30 says the killing was "counted to them for righteousness", and the Testament of Levi says Levi acted by an angel's command. The Hasmoneans, Levites themselves, fought the Samaritans of Shechem, and John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple on Mount Gerizim about 111 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255–256). For first readers the parallel was clear: a trick, an outrage against Israel's purity, and a sword. Judith's prayer also gives a precedent for deceit, since the brothers' trick is the model for her own.

Judith asks God to strike the enemy "by the deceit of my lips" (9:10) and "my words and my deceit" (9:13). She does not hide it, and the narrator never criticizes her. Readers have answered in several ways.

Every lie is wrong, but her purpose was good. Augustine held that it is never right to lie, even to save a life (On Lying). Aquinas followed him and explained the praise of Judith this way: "Judith is praised, not for lying to Holofernes, but for her desire to save the people, for which she put herself in danger" (Summa II-II q.110 a.3 ad 3). Jerome's Latin removed the word: the Douay reads "strike him by the graces of the words of my lips" (Douay 9:13).

Deceiving an enemy in war is not a lie in the forbidden sense. John Cassian allowed that holy men had sometimes used deceit for a greater good (Conferences 17), and some Protestant teachers, such as Charles Hodge, argued that deceiving an enemy in war, who has no right to the truth, is not a sinful lie (Systematic Theology, vol. 3, on the ninth commandment).

Stratagem, not falsehood. Aquinas also asked whether ambushes are lawful in war, and drew a line: one may hide one's plans from an enemy and lay traps, but may not tell him falsehoods or break a promise (Summa II-II q.40 a.3). On that line Judith's feint at dawn (14:2) is lawful, and her false story about her people's sin (11:11–15) is not.

Comparison. The Bible tells of other deceptions that saved lives. The midwives told Pharaoh, "It's because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women" (Exodus 1:19), and "God treated the midwives well" (Exodus 1:20). God himself gave Samuel a cover story to anoint David (1 Samuel 16:2). Rahab hid the spies and misled the king's men (Joshua 2:4–5). Whether a lie to save life can be right is carded at Joshua 2; whether an angel's disguise was deceit is carded at Tobit 12. Judith adds one thing these stories lack: a prayer asking God to make the deceit succeed. The book treats deceit as a weapon of war, like the sword.

echoes: Genesis 34; Genesis 49:5–7; Exodus 15:3; Exodus 1:19–20; Joshua 2:4–6; 1 Samuel 16:2; Judges 4:9; Judges 9:54; Psalm 20:7; Psalm 141:2; 1 Samuel 2:4–8; Luke 1:51–53; Isaiah 31:1

settings.to: God, alone in her rooftop tent
settings.when: at the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem, on the night she goes to the enemy
settings.why: To ask God to act through her hand and her deceit, to break the pride of an army that means to defile his Temple, and to show all nations that he alone protects Israel.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers (see the card at 8:11–27), the prayer named their own fear, a foreign army that would defile the sanctuary (9:8), and their own heroes' zeal (9:4). It taught them that God saves through the weak, as he had saved them through a few Maccabees.
views: Most readers take the prayer as trust in the God of the lowly.
A prayer for deceit and vengeance
Many readers, ancient and modern, have found its plea for deceit and its praise of Shechem morally troubling; Aquinas separated her motive from her lie.

title: Judith Goes Down to the Enemy
sum: Judith rises from prayer, takes off her sackcloth and widow's clothes, bathes, perfumes herself, and dresses in the festive clothes of her married life and all her jewelry, "to catch the eye of any man who might see her". With her maid carrying a bag of clean food, she goes to the gate, where the elders bless her, and out into the night.

An Assyrian patrol stops her. She says she is a Hebrew fleeing her people, with a way for Holofernes to take the hill country without losing a man. Her beauty does the rest. A hundred men escort her to the general's tent, and the whole camp comes running to see her. The soldiers say that the Hebrews, whose women look like this, should not be left alive, or they will outwit the whole world. Holofernes is resting on his bed under a canopy of purple and gold. Judith falls down before him.

views.C: Catholic readers followed Jerome's Latin, which adds that "the Lord also gave her more beauty: because all this dressing up did not proceed from sensuality, but from virtue" (Douay 10:4). Her adornment was read as obedience to God's plan, and her chastity as unharmed.
views.O: Orthodox readers have honored Judith's courage and her keeping of the food laws in the enemy camp, as a model of faith that keeps God's commands in the midst of danger.
views.P: Protestant readers have praised her courage; some have found her use of seduction a weakness in the book's morality.
views.H: Scholars see a deliberate reversal of the mourning widow: she returns to her married beauty to become a weapon. The scene is shaped by Esther and Ruth, and the soldiers' reaction is a comic touch: the whole army is beaten by one woman before a blow is struck.
views.J: Medieval Hebrew retellings kept the bag of food, often adding cheese and wine, which became the source of the custom of eating dairy foods on Hanukkah.

deep.b:
The narrator says plainly that Judith "made herself very beautiful, to catch the eye of any man who might see her" (10:4), and some manuscripts say "to deceive" (see the variant). Her beauty is praised by everyone who meets her (10:7, 14, 19, 23; 11:21, 23). Her beauty is praised more often than any other heroine's in these books, and it does what an army could not.

Christian writers wanted to hold together her beauty, her deceit and her chastity. Jerome's Latin answers that God himself increased her beauty because she acted from virtue, not from lust (Vulgate 10:4). Ambrose of Milan praised her in On Widows as a widow who, by sobriety, beat a drunken general, and Jerome held her up to the widow Furia as a model of chaste widowhood (Letter 54). Modern readers are divided. Some admire a woman who used the only weapon her world allowed her and kept her honor; others ask whether the story makes a woman's body an instrument of war. The book itself insists that she was not defiled (13:16) and that she lived chaste to the end (16:22).

echoes: Ruth 3:3; Esther 5:1; Esther 2:15–17; 1 Samuel 25:18–35; Daniel 1:8; Exodus 1:10; Genesis 40:15; Jonah 1:9

settings.what: The elders' blessing and Judith's order
settings.by: Uzziah and the elders, then Judith
settings.to: Judith, at the town gate; then Judith to the elders
settings.when: as she comes to the gate dressed for the enemy camp, the night after her prayer
settings.why: The elders bless her plan without knowing it; Judith orders the gate opened so she can carry out what they agreed. (The robing in 10:3–5 is narrated, not spoken.)
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, the elders' blessing, "for the delight of the Israelites and the honor of Jerusalem", gave the reader words that would be fulfilled when Jerusalem's leaders blessed Judith (15:9).

settings.to: the Assyrian scouts who stop her in the valley
settings.when: as she comes down through the valley, the night she leaves the town (8:33; 10:10–11)
settings.why: To pass the patrol with a story of flight and an offer of help, so they will take her to Holofernes. Her first words, "I am a daughter of the Hebrews", are true.

settings.when: after her answer
settings.why: To reassure her and to send her to Holofernes. Their promise that he will treat her well is the first of many promises that the reader knows are hollow.

settings.when: as they crowd around Judith outside the general's tent
settings.why: To express their wonder at her beauty, and their resolve not to leave a man of such a people alive. Unknowing, they name the danger that is already among them.

title: Judith's Story to Holofernes
sum: Holofernes promises Judith safety. In reply she makes the longest speech of her mission. She will not lie to "my lord" tonight. Achior was right: the Hebrews cannot be beaten unless they sin. But now, starving, they are about to sin, eating the animals the law forbids and the firstfruits and tithes kept for the priests. When they do, they will be handed over.

She will stay in the camp, go out each night to pray, and tell him when God reveals that they have sinned. Then she will lead him through Judea to Jerusalem and set his throne there. Holofernes and his officers are dazzled by her beauty and wisdom. If she does as she says, he promises, "your God will be my God".
readings: Read as irony

Almost every sentence Judith speaks can be heard two ways. "My lord" is Holofernes to him, God to her. God "will bring this matter to a full end" with him. The reader enjoys the trap that the hearer cannot see.
Read as deception
Not every line can be saved by double meaning. Her claim that Bethulia is about to sin is simply false, and she knows it. This is the chapter on which debates over Judith's lies have chiefly turned.

views.C: Catholic readers have mostly read the chapter with Aquinas, who taught that Judith's lie was not praiseworthy in itself but that her zeal for her people was (Summa II-II q.110 a.3 ad 3). Some Catholic commentators argued that many of her words were true in a sense Holofernes did not catch.
views.O: The Orthodox Church has made no ruling on Judith's speech. One strand of Greek patristic teaching allowed a deception told for another's salvation: John Chrysostom defended his own trick on his friend Basil that way (On the Priesthood 1.8–9). Read by that strand, 11:5–19 would be a saving stratagem.
views.P: Protestant writers often cited this chapter, with 9:10, as a moral reason for not treating Judith as Scripture. Others, like Charles Hodge, argued that deceiving an enemy in war is not a sinful lie (Systematic Theology, vol. 3).
views.H: Scholars admire the craft of the speech: flattery, a show of piety, a confirmation of Achior, an invented sin, and a prophecy. Its invented sin reflects real debates about food under siege in the Maccabean wars.
views.J: Jewish law permits much to save life, and medieval Hebrew retellings kept Judith's trick with admiration.

deep.b:
Judith says she "will not tell my lord a lie tonight" (11:5) and then tells a long and detailed falsehood: that her people are about to sin and that God will tell her when (11:11–17). Some of her lines are true in a hidden sense, but the core of the story is false. The book praises her for it.

The Bible gives other cases of deception for a good end. The Hebrew midwives answered Pharaoh with a story, and "God treated the midwives well" (Exodus 1:19–20). When Samuel feared Saul, God told him, "Say, 'I have come to offer a sacrifice to the LORD'" (1 Samuel 16:2), a true statement that hid his real errand. Rahab hid the spies and sent their pursuers the wrong way (Joshua 2:4–6), and Hebrews and James praise her faith and her works (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). Judith's speech goes further: it is a planned deception, made in prayer, and full of the name of God.

Whether a lie to save life can ever be right is set out in the card at Joshua 2, where the churches' answers are compared. Whether an angel deceived in human form is carded at Tobit 12. The deep section on chapter 9 sets out how Augustine, Aquinas, Cassian and later Protestants read Judith's prayer for deceit.

Judith swears "as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, lives" (11:7). The book makes him king of the Assyrians in Nineveh (1:1), but the real Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon (605–562 BC), Nineveh fell in 612 BC to his father and the Medes, and the Temple had not yet been rebuilt (compare 4:3). Most scholars read these as deliberate signals that the book is a story, not a chronicle; some think it was written in code for a later tyrant. The book's introduction discusses the question, and the card in book.json asks whether the story must have happened as told.

echoes: Exodus 1:19–20; 1 Samuel 16:2; Joshua 2:4–6; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25; Jeremiah 27:6; Daniel 2:38; Exodus 11:7; Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Ruth 1:16; Leviticus 22:10–16

settings.to: Judith, in his tent before his officers
settings.when: as she lies prostrate before him on her arrival
settings.why: To put her at ease and win her trust: whoever serves Nebuchadnezzar is safe, and her people brought the war on themselves.
settings.readers: The book's first readers had heard such promises from foreign kings and generals before (1 Maccabees 7:10–15, 27). The book shows the falseness of the tyrant's claim to be "king of the whole earth".

settings.when: on her arrival in the camp
settings.why: To win his trust and buy time: by flattering him, confirming Achior's warning, inventing the sin that will hand Israel over, and setting up her nightly freedom to go out "to pray".
views: Many readers hold that the speech is deceit in war, praised for its purpose; Aquinas separated her motive from the lie.
Others stress that much of it is true in a hidden sense, though not all.

settings.when: as she finishes speaking
settings.why: To marvel at her beauty and wisdom. The praise shows how completely the camp has been taken in.

settings.when: after her speech
settings.why: To accept her offer, thank "God" for sending her, and promise her honor in Nebuchadnezzar's house. His "your God will be my God" is a bargain, not a conversion.

title: Three Days in the Camp
sum: Holofernes offers Judith his own food and wine. She refuses: she will eat only what she brought, so that it will not be a stumbling block. When he asks what will happen when her food runs out, she swears that it will not run out before "he" has done by her hand what he planned. For three nights she goes out to the spring in the ravine, bathes, and prays for God to guide her way.

On the fourth day Holofernes gives a banquet for his household and sends Bagoas, his eunuch, to bring the Hebrew woman: it would be a disgrace not to sleep with such a woman. Judith dresses in all her finery, comes and reclines on fleeces before him, and eats and drinks only what her maid has prepared. Holofernes is overwhelmed with desire, and drinks more wine than he has ever drunk in one day.

views.C: Catholic writers saw in Judith's refusal of the general's food and her nightly prayer the pattern of a soul that keeps itself pure in the world.
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in Judith's fasting from the enemy's food a model of the faithful who keep the church's fasts even among unbelievers.
views.P: Protestant readers value the chapter's example of keeping God's law under pressure, and of prayer, while not making the food laws binding on Christians (Romans 14).
views.H: Scholars see the chapter as a careful build-up of suspense and irony. Judith's food laws and washings reflect Jewish practice of the Greek period, like Daniel 1 and the Letter of Aristeas. The banquet is pictured as a Greek symposium.
views.J: Judith's refusal of Gentile food is a model of faithfulness found also in Daniel, Tobit and Esther. Medieval Jewish retellings expanded the banquet scene, with the cheese and wine that made the general drunk.

deep.h: Food laws in the enemy's tent
deep.b:
Judith's refusal is the high point of a theme in the Jewish books of the Greek period. Daniel set his heart on "not defiling himself with the king's rich food" (Daniel 1:8); Tobit says that while his kin ate "the food of the Gentiles", he kept himself from it (Tobit 1:10–11); in the Greek Esther, the queen has not eaten at Haman's table nor drunk the wine of libations (Additions to Esther 14:17). During Antiochus IV's persecution, many in Israel refused unclean food and accepted death instead (1 Maccabees 1:62–63), as the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7 did. Judith keeps the law even while she deceives and prepares to kill, and her clean food bag becomes the sack for the general's head (13:10). For the book, faithfulness to the law and courage in war go together.

Christians read the chapter in the light of Jesus' teaching that food does not defile (Mark 7:18–19) and Paul's rule not to put a stumbling block in another's way (Romans 14:13–21). The book's word for that, skandalon, is the same as Judith's (12:2).

echoes: Daniel 1:8–16; Tobit 1:10–11; 1 Maccabees 1:62–63; Romans 14:13–21; Mark 7:18–19; Esther 5:4–8; 1 Samuel 25:26; Genesis 12:15; Genesis 34:2

settings.to: each other, in the room where his silver was kept
settings.when: when he orders his own food and wine served to her
settings.why: For Judith, to keep the food laws and to give a sworn promise, with a hidden meaning, that God will act before her food runs out.
settings.readers: Many of the book's first readers remembered the martyrs who died rather than eat forbidden food (1 Maccabees 1:62–63; 2 Maccabees 6–7). Judith showed them a heroine who kept the law even in the enemy's tent.

settings.when: before dawn on her first morning
settings.why: To make her nightly going out a routine, so that on the last night the guards will let her pass.

settings.when: on the fourth day, as he prepares a banquet for his household
settings.why: To bring Judith to the banquet so that he can sleep with her; he fears she will laugh at him if he does not.

settings.when: in her tent on the fourth day
settings.why: Bagoas invites her to drink with the general and be like the Assyrian women of the palace; Judith agrees in words that can be heard as a vow to God.

settings.when: as she reclines before him at the banquet
settings.why: Holofernes urges her to drink and be merry; she answers with another double meaning, that this is the greatest day of her life.

title: The Head of Holofernes
sum: Late at night the servants leave, and Bagoas shuts the tent. Judith is alone with Holofernes, who lies on his bed, dead drunk. Standing by him, she prays silently: "Lord, God of all power, at this hour look upon what my hands are doing." She takes his sword from the bedpost, grasps his hair, prays "Make me strong today, God of Israel!", and strikes his neck twice. She rolls the body off the bed, takes down the canopy, and gives the head to her maid, who puts it in the food bag.

The two women walk out of the camp as they do every night, climb to Bethulia, and call for the gate to be opened. The whole town gathers by firelight. Judith shows them the head and the canopy and praises God, who struck him down "by a woman's hand" and kept her from defilement. The people worship God, and Uzziah blesses her as "blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth".
readings: Read as a story of deliverance

The killing is the climax the whole book has prepared. God answers Judith's prayer, and the enemy who wanted to "destroy the whole earth" dies at the hands of a widow. Jews and Christians have retold it as one of the great deliverances, like Jael's and David's.
Read with modern unease

Modern readers ask what kind of violence the book blesses: a prayer, a deception, and a killing in God's name. Some read it as a just act against an invader; others see a story that, read carelessly, can justify killing in God's name.

views.C: Catholic tradition read the beheading as a figure of the victory of humility and chastity over pride, and of Mary's victory over the serpent (Genesis 3:15), and sings Uzziah's blessing of Mary (see the card on chapter 15). Jerome's Latin adds that an angel guarded her, so that she came back "without pollution of sin" (Douay 13:20).
views.O: Orthodox readers have honored Judith as a deliverer of God's people, read with the Septuagint, and have seen in her a figure of courage given by God to the weak.
views.P: Protestant readers have praised her courage; some have criticized the deceit. On whether Christians may resist an unjust ruler, see the card at 1 Samuel 24.
views.H: Scholars see the scene shaped by Jael (Judges 4–5), David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17) and Ehud (Judges 3). The display of the head recalls Nicanor's head hung in Jerusalem in 161 BC (1 Maccabees 7:47), within living memory of the book's first readers.
views.J: In the medieval Hebrew retellings, Judith beheads the enemy king and the Jews celebrate. Rashi and the Tosafot linked her deed with the miracle of Hanukkah (see chapter 16).

deep.b:
Judith's deed is told in a single verse: two blows, and the head is off (13:8). The story does not linger on blood, but it does not apologize. She prays before she strikes, and God is praised for it (13:14, 17). The model is Jael, who drove a tent peg through the sleeping Sisera's temple: "She struck Sisera, she smashed his head, / she broke through and split his temple" (Judges 5:26). David cut off Goliath's head with Goliath's own sword (1 Samuel 17:51), and Ehud killed King Eglon in a locked room (Judges 3:21).

As a just act of war. Most Jewish and Christian readers through history praised Judith as a deliverer. Holofernes led an army that had destroyed temples and peoples (3:8) and was about to destroy Judea (2:7–13). The Catholic tradition of just war, from Augustine to Aquinas, allowed killing in defense of the people under public authority (Summa II-II q.40), and Judith's deed was approved by the town's rulers.

As tyrannicide. In the Middle Ages and the Reformation, Judith became an example in debates over killing a tyrant. After Florence expelled the Medici in 1494, Donatello's bronze of Judith was set up before the town hall in 1495 as a warning to tyrants. Whether Christians may resist an unjust ruler is carded at 1 Samuel 24.

With unease. Many modern readers, after centuries of violence done in God's name, are troubled by a story in which a prayer for deceit and a killing are blessed by God. Some answer that the book is a story of a weak people saved from genocide and should not be read as a model for private violence. Others read it as a symbol: Judith is Judea, and her victory is God's. Whether Christians may fight in war is carded at Deuteronomy 20, and Joshua's wars at the book of Joshua.

echoes: Judges 4:17–22; Judges 5:24–27; Judges 3:15–25; 1 Samuel 17:51–54; 1 Samuel 1:13; Judges 16:28; Genesis 14:19–20; Luke 1:42; Genesis 3:15; 1 Maccabees 7:47; Isaiah 7:14

settings.what: Judith's silent prayer by the bed
settings.when: alone in Holofernes' bedroom, as he lies drunk
settings.why: To ask God to look on her hands and give her strength to act for Jerusalem and for his inheritance.
settings.readers: The book's first readers knew that the Temple had been saved by a small band who prayed and fought (1 Maccabees 4:10–11, 30–33). Judith's silent prayer made her act the answer to prayer, not merely a killing.

settings.when: as she takes hold of his hair, sword in hand
settings.why: To ask for strength for the blow, in Samson's words (Judges 16:28).

settings.to: the guards, then the whole town of Bethulia, gathered by firelight
settings.when: on her return from the camp in the night
settings.why: To have the gate opened, to call the town to praise God, to show the head and the canopy as proof, and to declare that she was not defiled.

settings.what: The people's praise and Uzziah's blessing
settings.when: after she shows the head
settings.why: To bless God for bringing the enemy to nothing, and to bless Judith "above all the women on earth", praising her courage in risking her life. The people answer "So be it! So be it!"
views: In the story, the blessing follows those of Jael (Judges 5:24) and Abram (Genesis 14:19–20).
Catholic tradition hears it as a figure of Elizabeth's blessing of Mary (Luke 1:42) and sings it of her (see the card on chapter 15).

title: Achior Believes
sum: Judith gives the battle plan. Hang the head on the wall. At dawn let every man take his weapons and march out as if to attack, but not go down. The Assyrians will rush to wake Holofernes, find him dead, and run. First, though, she calls for Achior the Ammonite. When he sees the head of the man who sent him to Bethulia to die, he faints, then falls at her feet and blesses her. He hears her story, believes in God completely, is circumcised, and joins the house of Israel.

At dawn the head hangs on the wall and the Israelites march out. The Assyrian officers send to wake their general. Bagoas knocks, then goes in and finds the headless body on the floor. He cries out and tears his clothes, searches Judith's tent and finds it empty, and runs out shouting: "One Hebrew woman has brought shame on the house of King Nebuchadnezzar!" The camp is thrown into panic.

views.C: Some Catholic readers have seen Achior as a figure of the Gentiles who come to faith, believing first and then receiving the sign of the covenant.
views.O: Orthodox readers have read Achior's conversion as a figure of the nations' turning to the true God, and his believing before circumcision as faith that receives the sign.
views.P: Protestant readers have noticed that Achior believes and is then circumcised, the order Paul stresses for Abraham (Romans 4:9–12), and that his conversion conflicts with Deuteronomy 23:3, which some count among the book's difficulties.
views.H: Scholars note that Achior's conversion fits the Hasmonean period, when circumcision marked joining Israel and the Hasmoneans required it of the Idumeans and Itureans. His Ammonite origin, against Deuteronomy 23:3, may be a deliberate statement that faith outweighs birth.
views.J: Jewish law discussed Achior's case. The Mishnah allowed an Ammonite convert, Judah, to enter the community because Sennacherib had mixed up the nations (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4), and the Talmud limited the ban on Ammonites to men (Yevamot 76b–77a).

deep.b:
The law says: "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of their descendants may ever enter the assembly of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 23:3). Nehemiah read that law to the people and they separated from all foreigners (Nehemiah 13:1–3). Yet Judith ends Achior's story with the words "he was joined to the house of Israel, to this day" (14:10). On its face the book conflicts with Deuteronomy.

Jewish teachers found ways to read the two together. The Mishnah tells of "Judah, an Ammonite convert", who asked whether he could enter the assembly. Rabbi Joshua said yes, because Sennacherib king of Assyria had mixed up all the nations, so that the Ammonites of Moses' day no longer existed (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4). The Talmud also read the ban as applying only to men, which is how Ruth the Moabite could marry Boaz (Yevamot 76b–77a). Prophets had already promised that foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would not be cut off (Isaiah 56:3–7).

Achior's order, faith first and then circumcision, matches Abram, who "put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6) before he was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul builds his argument on that order (Romans 4:9–12). For Judith, though, circumcision is still necessary: it is how a believing Gentile joins Israel. That fits the Hasmonean age, when John Hyrcanus required the Idumeans to be circumcised (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258).

echoes: Deuteronomy 23:3; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:3–7; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 17:10–14; Romans 4:9–12; Esther 8:17; 1 Samuel 31:10; 1 Maccabees 7:47; Judges 7:19–22

settings.to: the men of Bethulia, gathered at the gate in the night
settings.when: after she shows them the head
settings.why: To turn the death of the general into a rout: a feint at dawn that will send the Assyrians to find him dead. She also asks for Achior, so that he can see the head.
settings.readers: The book's first readers had seen Judah Maccabee win by surprise and by small numbers (1 Maccabees 4:1–25). Judith's plan, with God's panic on the enemy, followed the pattern of Gideon and Jonathan.

settings.when: when he recovers from fainting at the sight of the head
settings.why: To honor Judith and to ask for her story; his blessing prepares for his faith.

settings.to: the one in charge of Holofernes' affairs, Bagoas
settings.when: at dawn, when the Israelites march out
settings.why: To have their general woken to fight the "slaves" who have come out to attack.

settings.when: after he finds Holofernes' body and Judith gone
settings.why: To raise the alarm; his words state the book's point: one Hebrew woman has shamed the house of Nebuchadnezzar.

title: Jerusalem Blesses Judith
sum: Panic seizes the leaderless Assyrian army, and it flees by every road. Uzziah sends messengers through the land, and the men of Israel pour out from Bethulia, Jerusalem, the hill country, Gilead and Galilee, chasing the enemy past Damascus. For thirty days the people plunder the camp, and Judith receives Holofernes' tent and all his silver.

Joakim the high priest and the council of elders come from Jerusalem to see what God has done and to bless Judith: "You are Jerusalem's honor! You are Israel's great delight! You are our people's great boast!" The women of Israel come running to dance in her honor. Crowned with olive leaves and carrying leafy wands, Judith leads the women in the dance, and the men follow, armed and garlanded, singing.

views.C: The Catholic liturgy applies the elders' praise (15:9–10) and Uzziah's blessing (13:18) to Mary, above all on the feast of the Immaculate Conception. Judith is read as a figure of the Virgin who, by God's grace, crushes the enemy's head. See the card below.
views.O: Orthodox readers honor Judith with the other holy women of the Old Testament. Orthodox hymnography has many Old Testament figures of the Theotokos, but no regular use of Judith's praises is known in the Byzantine services.
views.P: Protestant churches do not use Judith's praises of Mary and reject any doctrine of Mary grounded on the Apocrypha. Luther read the whole book as an allegory of the Jewish people.
views.H: Scholars note the victory procession and the high priest's role, which fit the Hasmonean age. The ivy-wreathed thyrsus also appears at the purification of the Temple in 164 BC (2 Maccabees 10:7), which suggests a link with the feast that became Hanukkah.
views.J: Jewish readers recognized in the victory celebration and the role of the high priest the world of the Maccabees, and in the Middle Ages the story was read at Hanukkah.

deep.b:
Uzziah's blessing, "you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth" (13:18), joins Deborah's blessing of Jael, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24), and Melchizedek's blessing of Abram (Genesis 14:19–20). Elizabeth's greeting to Mary, "Blessed are you among women" (Luke 1:42), uses the same form. Medieval Latin writers read Judith as a figure of Mary: a woman, chaste and humble, through whom God strikes the head of the enemy, as promised in Genesis 3:15. Medieval picture books of salvation set Judith beheading Holofernes beside Mary overcoming the devil.

In the Roman liturgy, the Gradual of the Mass of the Immaculate Conception in the Missal used before 1970 sang the Latin of Uzziah's blessing with "Virgin Mary" for "daughter", and then the elders' praise (Vulgate 13:23; 15:10): Benedicta es tu, Virgo Maria, a Domino Deo excelso, prae omnibus mulieribus super terram. V. Tu gloria Ierusalem, tu laetitia Israel, tu honorificentia populi nostri. The antiphon Tota pulchra es uses the same three titles. In today's Liturgy of the Hours, a canticle from Judith's song (16:2–3a, 13–15 in the breviary's numbering; 16:1–2a, 13–15 in this site's) is sung at Morning Prayer on Wednesday of Week I, and in the lectionary used in the United States, Judith 13:18–19 is the responsorial psalm on the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe, with a response taken from 15:9. The churches' views of this reading are set out in the card below; whether Mary is the woman of Genesis 3:15 is carded at Genesis 3.

echoes: Judges 5:24; Genesis 14:19–20; Luke 1:42; Luke 1:48; Genesis 3:15; Exodus 15:20–21; 1 Samuel 18:6–7; 2 Maccabees 10:6–7; 1 Maccabees 5:9–23; Judges 7:22–24

settings.by: Joakim the high priest and the council of elders of Jerusalem
settings.to: Judith, in Bethulia, with all the people
settings.when: when they come from Jerusalem after the victory
settings.why: To honor her publicly as the glory of the nation and to bless her before the Lord Almighty. The words fulfill the elders' blessing at the gate (10:8). The people answer "So be it!"
settings.readers: In the book's first readers' day, the high priest and the council of elders ruled the nation from Jerusalem, as here. In the book, the highest authorities of Judaism honor a woman of Bethulia who saved the Temple.
views: In the story, the leaders praise Judith as the nation's savior.
Catholic worship sings these words of Mary (see the card).

traditions.q: Catholic worship sings Uzziah's blessing (13:18) and the elders' praise (15:9–10) of Mary. Is Judith a figure of Mary, and may the church use her praises that way? (Whether Mary is the woman of Genesis 3:15 is carded at Genesis 3.)
views: Yes. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Old Testament, read in the light of later revelation, brings "the figure of the woman, Mother of the Redeemer" into gradually clearer light (Lumen Gentium 55), and Judith, the woman through whom God struck the enemy's head, is a figure of Mary. The Roman Missal used until 1970 sang "Benedicta es tu, Virgo Maria, a Domino Deo excelso, prae omnibus mulieribus super terram" with "Tu gloria Ierusalem, tu laetitia Israel, tu honorificentia populi nostri" in the Gradual of the Immaculate Conception (a Mass of 1863). The same titles are sung in the antiphon Tota pulchra es, and the current lectionary (in the United States) uses Judith 13:18–19 as the psalm on the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. The Liturgy of the Hours sings Judith's song at Morning Prayer on Wednesday of Week I.

No doctrine from it. Luther's preface reads Judith as an allegory of the Jewish people (Judea) and Holofernes as the godless ruler, not as Mary. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession honors Mary and the saints but rejects calling on them and transferring to them what belongs to Christ (article 21).

title: Judith's Song
sum: Judith leads all Israel in a song of thanks. She calls for tambourines and cymbals, then tells how Assyria came down from the north with countless troops to burn and kill, and how the Lord Almighty brought them to nothing "by a woman's hand". No young men, Titans or giants struck the enemy down. Judith, Merari's daughter, did it with the beauty of her face. The song ends with a hymn to the creator, before whom mountains melt like wax, who values those who fear him above all sacrifice, and who will punish the nations that rise against his people with fire and worms forever.

In Jerusalem the people purify themselves and offer sacrifices. Judith dedicates the canopy and all Holofernes' goods to God. The rejoicing lasts three months. Then Judith goes home to Bethulia. Many men want to marry her, but she remains a widow all her life. She frees her maid, lives to 105, and is buried with her husband. As long as she lives, and long after, no one makes Israel afraid.
readings: Read as a new Song of the Sea
The song echoes Exodus 15 and Judges 5: a woman leads the dance, the enemy's pride is told, and God is praised as the one who shatters wars.
Read as the book's summary
The song retells the story in poetry, turning it from Judith's deed to God's glory as creator and judge.

views.C: Catholic worship sings part of the song (16:2–3a, 13–15 in the breviary's numbering; 16:1–2a, 13–15 in this site's) in the Liturgy of the Hours. Judith's lifelong widowhood was held up as a model of chastity, which Jerome's Latin stresses: "chastity was joined to her virtue" (Douay 16:26).
views.O: Orthodox readers have the song in their Greek Old Testament. Judith's refusal to remarry fits Orthodox respect for widows who do not remarry, though the church allows a second marriage.
views.P: Protestant readers have valued the song as a hymn of praise like the Psalms, but read 16:17 with care, and have not taken Judith's widowhood as a higher calling than marriage.
views.H: Scholars think the song may be older than the story, perhaps from a Hebrew original, built on Exodus 15 and Judges 5. The fire and worms of 16:17 are among the earliest Jewish statements of conscious, lasting punishment.
views.J: Medieval Jewish tradition linked Judith with Hanukkah, and many medieval Hebrew poems and stories retold her deed. The Vulgate's claim that her victory became a Jewish holy day (16:31) is not supported by Jewish sources.

deep.b:
Judith's song stands in a line with the Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah.

Exodus 15. Moses and Israel sing, "Horse and its rider / he has flung into the sea" (Exodus 15:1), and Miriam leads the women with tambourine and dance (Exodus 15:20–21). Judith takes the women's part and speaks in the first person like Moses. She quotes the Greek of Exodus 15:3 (16:2), as she did in her prayer: "the Lord who shatters wars" (9:7); and her picture of the enemy's boasts (16:4) is like Pharaoh's "I'll chase, I'll catch, / I'll split up the spoil" (Exodus 15:9).

Judges 5. Deborah sings, "I, yes I, will sing to the LORD" (Judges 5:3), and blesses Jael above women (Judges 5:24), telling her deed in close detail (Judges 5:26–27). Judith's song tells her own deed in the third person, from her sandal to the sword (16:9). Both end with the land at peace (Judges 5:31; 16:25).

What is new. Judith's song adds a hymn to the creator (16:13–15) like Psalms 33 and 104, and the claim that fear of the Lord is worth more than all sacrifice (16:16). It closes with judgment on the nations, fire and worms forever (16:17), going beyond Isaiah 66:24. Whether final punishment is endless conscious suffering is carded at 1 Enoch 108 and Jude 1.

Judith is not a Hanukkah book in the ancient sources. The Greek never mentions the feast, and Jerome's claim that "the day of the festivity of this victory is received by the Hebrews in the number of holy days" (Douay 16:31) has no support in Jewish sources. But the book was likely written for readers who knew the Maccabean victories, and its procession with leafy wands (15:12) recalls the first Hanukkah, when the people carried the same thyrsi at the purification of the Temple (2 Maccabees 10:7; compare 1 Maccabees 4:52–59).

The link became explicit in the Middle Ages. Medieval Hebrew retellings set Judith's deed in the time of the Maccabees, and some were read at Hanukkah. Rashi explained the Talmud's saying that women were obliged in the Hanukkah lights because "they too were part of the miracle" (Shabbat 23a) by the story of a woman who saved Israel, and the Tosafot named her Judith (Tosafot on Megillah 4a). Moses Isserles (the Rema) recorded the custom of eating cheese on Hanukkah, because the miracle was done through the milk Judith fed the enemy (gloss to Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 670:2). Jerome's Latin mentions cheese among her provisions (Vulgate 10:5).

"Many men desired her, but no man slept with her all the days of her life" (16:22). Judith chose not to remarry, though the law gave her freedom to. Paul allowed a widow to marry, but thought her more fortunate if she stayed as she was (1 Corinthians 7:40), and he praised the widow who "stays with her pleas and prayers night and day" (1 Timothy 5:5), like Anna in the Temple (Luke 2:36–37). Ambrose of Milan, in On Widows, held up Judith as an example, and Jerome used her when he urged the young widow Furia not to remarry (Letter 54). The churches differ on whether widowhood and celibacy are a higher calling; see the card below.

echoes: Exodus 15:1–21; Judges 5:1–31; Psalm 33:6–9; Psalm 104:30; Psalm 97:5; Psalm 51:16–17; 1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:48; 2 Maccabees 10:6–7; 1 Corinthians 7:39–40; 1 Timothy 5:5; Luke 2:36–37; Judges 5:31

settings.by: Judith, with all the people singing after her (15:14)
settings.to: God, before all Israel, in the victory procession on the way to Jerusalem
settings.when: after the rout of the Assyrians and the thirty days of plunder
settings.why: To give the glory to God: to retell the victory in poetry, to praise the creator who saves the weak, and to warn the nations who attack God's people.
settings.readers: The song gave the book's first readers a hymn for their own victories, in the old forms of Miriam and Deborah, and a warning to the nations that God would judge those who attacked his people.
views: Most readers hear it as a victory hymn in the tradition of Exodus 15 and Judges 5.
Some scholars think the song was composed first, in Hebrew, and the story built around it.

traditions.q: Judith never remarried, and "no man slept with her all the days of her life" (16:22). Is lifelong widowhood or celibacy a higher calling than marriage?
views: Yes, as a gift for the kingdom. The Council of Trent condemned anyone who says that marriage is to be placed above virginity or celibacy, and that it is not better and more blessed to remain in virginity or celibacy (Session 24, canon 10). The Catechism teaches that virginity for the sake of the kingdom and marriage both come from the Lord and support each other (CCC 1618–1620), and that the church has honored consecrated virgins and widows from apostolic times (CCC 922).

Remaining unmarried after a spouse's death is honored, and remarriage is allowed but treated as a concession. The church permits a second, and even a third, marriage, with a more penitential service than the first, and its clergy may not remarry (Ware, The Orthodox Church).

A gift, not a higher state that earns merit. The Augsburg Confession teaches that celibacy is a gift few have and rejects vows that make it a way of earning righteousness (articles 23, 27). The Apology grants that virginity is a more excellent gift than marriage, but denies that it justifies (article 23).

No higher state. The Second Helvetic Confession says that those who have the gift of celibacy from heaven may remain single, while those who do not should marry, and it condemns those who condemn second marriages (chapter 29).
